description: Weevils are plant-feeding beetles characterized by a long snout (rostrum). Both larvae and adults damage crops by feeding on plant tissues such as leaves, fruits, seeds, stems or roots. Many species are serious pests in agriculture and storage systems.
identification: Adults have a long curved snout called a rostrum
Elbowed antennae ending in a club
Body robust and usually covered with scales or bristles
Larvae are white, C-shaped grubs without legs
life_cycle: Female uses the rostrum to drill holes in plant tissue
Eggs are laid inside fruits, seeds, stems or roots
Larvae develop inside plant tissue and feed internally
Larvae pupate in soil or plant material
Adults emerge and continue feeding on plants
symptoms: Small holes in leaves, fruits or seeds
Damaged or hollow seeds and grains
Larval tunnels inside stems or fruits
Presence of adult beetles with a long snout
favorable_conditions: Fields with plant residues or poor sanitation
spread: Movement of infested seeds or fruits
Adult beetles flying to new host plants
Transport of contaminated soil or plant material
economic_importance: Major pests of agricultural crops worldwide
Can cause significant yield and quality losses
biological_control: Predators such as birds, spiders and predatory beetles
Parasitic wasps attacking larvae or eggs
Entomopathogenic fungi such as Beauveria bassiana and Metarhizium anisopliae
integrated_management: Crop rotation to break the life cycle
Remove and destroy infested fruits or plant residues
Use pheromone or food traps to monitor adults
Use resistant or tolerant crop varieties
Apply biological or chemical control when populations exceed thresholds
sources: Triplehorn & Johnson – Borror and DeLong's Introduction to the Study of Insects
